title: Sunksqua Weany
summary: Weany was a Shinnecock sunksquaw who marked the April 10, 1662 Topping agreement. Its whale-profit clause and a later protest by other Shinnecock landholders reveal the contested history of the Quogue and Canoe Place landscape.
content:
Weany and Shinnecock landholding

Weany was a seventeenth-century Shinnecock sunksquaw named in the agreement of April 10, 1662, concerning land west of Canoe Place toward Seatuck. She appears beside Anabackus and Jackanapes as one of the people making the bargain with Thomas Topping. Her mark places a Native woman at the center of a consequential South Shore transaction.1

The deed identifies the three principal Native parties as residents of Shinnecock near Southampton. It does not record Weany’s age or the dates of her birth and death. Her public role emerges through the land, resources, and obligations that she helped negotiate.1

April 10, 1662: the Topping agreement

The tract ran westward from Canoe Place, also called Niamuck, to Seatuck, then northward toward the head of the bay. The written conveyance included meadow, pasture, arable land, and other benefits. Topping was to pay eighty fathoms of wampum, or an equivalent, by the following December 1.1

Weany, Anabackus, and Jackanapes appear in the body of the deed; Wataugum, Tequobin, and Cobish also marked it. Those additional names matter because the payment was owed to the principal parties together with other interested Native people named below them.1

Whales and the value of the beach

The bargain included half the profits from whales cast onto the South Shore beach, as well as its grazing. The clause divided a valuable coastal benefit rather than giving Topping an unqualified claim to every whale. It connects Weany’s land diplomacy to the history of Indigenous whaling and maritime labor.1

The coast’s value lay in several activities at once: pasture, movement between bays and ocean, and the use of stranded whales. A land boundary alone therefore tells only part of what was being negotiated.1

September 17, 1666: other Shinnecock owners object

Four years later, other Shinnecock landholders formally protested the sale. They named Weany, Anabackus, and Jackanapes and asserted that the sellers lacked the right to convey the tract. They conditionally assigned their own interests to Southampton, with payment to follow if Governor Nicolls found their claim valid.1

The protest includes marks identified as Mandush’s son, Mandush’s daughter, and the wife of Goabes, described as Mandush’s widow, alongside other signers. Women thus appear on both sides of the title dispute. The document preserves a competing claim; it is not a record of Weany withdrawing hers.1

A wider contest over authority

Earlier, the 1659 Ogden agreement associated this same western Southampton landscape with Wyandanch and his son. The 1664 Montaukett–Shinnecock agreement subsequently recognized Quashawam while also addressing Shinnecock obligations. Weany’s deed and the 1666 protest show that local rights continued to be asserted alongside those broader arrangements.3 2 1

Following these documents in sequence brings several Native leaders into view and shows why the history of Quogue cannot be reduced to one purchaser and one sale.3 2 1

References

Supp. 2d 185 (E.D.N.Y. 2007), historical findings section E(1), Ogden Purchase, and notes 11–13: May 12, 1659 deed, September 19, 1666 Halsey/Sayre testimony, June 7, 1665 payment order. why_this_matters: Weany's record shows Indigenous women's leadership in land, law, and community sovereignty. Her presence makes visible a Shinnecock leader whose authority colonial histories too often reduce to a deed reference.
